title: Orders & the Order Book
tagline: Bids, asks and spreads, and the right order for each job.

levels.title: Bid, Ask & Spread
levels.summary: Every quote has two prices. The gap between them is a cost you pay on every round trip.
objectives: Identify the bid and the ask.
Calculate the spread and the spread %.
Explain why a round trip costs at least the spread.

terms.definition: The highest price a buyer is currently offering.
The lowest price a seller will currently accept. Also called the offer.
Ask − bid. A cost paid when you buy at the ask and sell at the bid.
Halfway between the bid and the ask.
How easily you can trade without moving the price. Liquid stocks have tight spreads.

cards.title: Two prices, not one
cards.body: A quote shows two prices. **Bid $49.95** is the highest price a buyer offers. **Ask $50.05** is the lowest price a seller accepts. Buy now and you pay the ask. Sell now and you receive the bid.

cards.title: The spread
cards.body: **Spread = ask − bid**, here $0.10. It is a hidden cost: buy at the ask, sell straight away at the bid, and you lose the spread on every share. 100 shares × $0.10 = $10 gone before the price has moved at all.

cards.title: Liquid versus thin
cards.body: Busy stocks have many buyers and sellers, so spreads are tight, often a cent or two. Thinly traded stocks have wide spreads. **Spread % = spread ÷ mid price.** A $0.10 spread on a $50 stock is 0.2%; a $0.40 spread on a $10 stock is 4%.

cards.title: The mid and the close
cards.body: The **mid** is halfway between bid and ask. Charts show each day's closing price. In this game a market buy pays the close plus half the spread and a market sell gets the close minus half. Holdings left at the end are valued at the final close.

cards.title: Costs you can't see
cards.body: Many real brokers advertise $0 commission, but you still pay the spread on every trade. In this game you also pay a fee of 0.1% of the order value, minimum $1. Each extra round trip pays both again.

check.prompt: Quote: Bid $24.80 / Ask $25.00. You market-buy 10 shares and enough are offered. What price do you pay?
check.explanation: Market buys fill at the ask.

check.prompt: Same quote: Bid $24.80 / Ask $25.00. What is the spread?
You buy 100 shares at $25.00 and immediately sell them at $24.80, with no commission. What is the result?
Which quote costs the most, as a percentage, to trade in and out of?
check.explanation: $0.50 on a $10.25 mid is about 5%; the others are 0.1% or less.

levels.title: Market Orders
levels.summary: Market orders trade price certainty for speed. Learn slippage and why gaps matter.
objectives: Explain that market orders trade price certainty for speed.
Recognize gap fills at the open.

terms.definition: An order to buy or sell now at the best available price.
The difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got.
The list of waiting buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) at each price.

cards.title: Buy now, whatever the price
cards.body: A **market order** fills straight away at the best available price: the ask for buys, the bid for sells. You get speed and near-certainty of a fill. You give up control over the exact price.

cards.title: Slippage
cards.body: If your order is bigger than the shares offered at the best ask, the rest fills at higher prices. The book shows 100 @ $50.05 and 200 @ $50.10. Buy 250: 100 × $50.05 + 150 × $50.10 = $12,520, an average of **$50.08**. That extra is **slippage**.

cards.title: Gaps
cards.body: In real markets, a market order sent after the close waits for the next open. If bad news lands overnight, the open can be far from the last close, and your order fills there. In this game you trade at the close you see, but a news gap is already in the price when you react.

cards.title: When to use one
cards.body: Use a market order when getting in or out matters more than a few cents, in a liquid stock with a tight spread. It is risky in thin stocks, where the spread is wide and the book is shallow, and in the minutes around big news.

check.prompt: What is the main advantage of a market order?

options.text: It executes quickly and almost certainly

check.explanation: Speed and certainty of a fill, not certainty of price.

check.prompt: Asks: 100 @ $20.00, 100 @ $20.05, 200 @ $20.10. You market-buy 300 shares. What is your average price?
In a real market, you send a market sell order in the evening after Day 9 closes at $30. Bad news arrives overnight and Day 10 opens at $27. Your fill is about:
check.explanation: The order waits for the open and fills at the gapped price.

check.prompt: A market order guarantees you the last traded price.
check.explanation: It fills at the best price available when it executes, which can differ.

levels.title: Limit Orders
levels.summary: Name your price. A limit order controls what you pay, but it may never fill.
objectives: Explain limit price rules for buys and sells.
Recognize that a limit order may never fill.
Use a sell limit as a take-profit.

terms.definition: An order to buy at or below, or sell at or above, a price you choose.
Buys only at your limit price or lower.
Sells only at your limit price or higher.
A sell limit above the current price that locks in a planned gain.

cards.title: Name your price
cards.body: A **buy limit** at $48 buys only at $48 or lower. A **sell limit** at $55 sells only at $55 or higher. You control the price; the market decides whether it ever gets there.

cards.title: The catch
cards.body: If the price never reaches your limit, nothing fills. Your buy limit sits at $45, the stock rallies from $47 to $55 without dipping, and you miss the whole move. Price control costs you certainty.

cards.title: How limits fill here
cards.body: A limit order placed today starts working tomorrow and waits until it fills or you cancel it. A buy limit fills on a day whose low reaches your price. If the stock opens below your limit, you get the better opening price. Limit fills pay the fee but not the spread.

cards.title: Take-profit
cards.body: A sell limit above the current price is a **profit target**. Bought Kestrel Air at $96 and aiming for $102? Place a sell limit at $102 and it fills on the first day the high reaches $102, even if you're not watching. Drag the line to see which day it would fill.

check.prompt: You think Kestrel Air will dip to $95.50 and want to buy only there or lower. Which order?
check.explanation: A buy limit fills only at your price or better.

check.prompt: Your buy limit is at $40. The next candle is Open 41.20, High 41.80, Low 40.30, Close 41.00. Does it fill?
Your buy limit is at $40. The next candle is Open 39.10, High 40.50, Low 38.90, Close 40.20. What is your fill price?
check.explanation: It opened below your limit, so you got the better opening price.

check.prompt: A sell limit at $60 can execute at $61.
check.explanation: A sell limit means "$60 or better", and $61 is better.

levels.title: Stop Orders & Stop-Losses
levels.summary: A tripwire that gets you out when you're wrong. Decide it before you buy.
objectives: Explain how a stop order triggers.
Place a stop-loss before entering a trade.
Recognize gap fills below the stop and the stop-limit trade-off.

terms.definition: An order that waits until a trigger price trades, then becomes a market order.
A sell stop below your entry that limits a losing trade.
A stop that becomes a limit order when triggered. It controls price but may not fill.
The chance that price jumps past your stop, so it fills at a worse price.

cards.title: A tripwire
cards.body: A **sell stop** at $45, with the price at $50, does nothing until the price trades at or below $45. Then it becomes a market sell. It waits quietly in the background so you don't have to watch every candle.

cards.title: Stop-loss
cards.body: A **stop-loss** limits a losing trade to roughly your planned level. Decide it **before** you buy. Buy 100 shares at $50 with a stop at $47 and your planned risk is about 100 × $3 = $300. The order ticket shows this as "risk if stopped".

cards.title: Gaps go through stops
cards.body: A stock closes at $46. Bad news arrives and it opens at $40. A stop at $45 fills near **$40**, not $45. A stop limits normal losses, but it is not a guaranteed price. That is why position size matters too.

cards.title: Buy stops and stop-limits
cards.body: Real brokers also offer a **buy stop** above the price, which buys when the price breaks upward, and a **stop-limit**, which becomes a limit once triggered: it protects your price but might not fill in a gap. In this game, stop orders are sell stop-losses.

cards.title: Where to place it
cards.body: Not so tight that normal daily wiggles hit it, and not so wide that the loss is huge. Just below a recent low is a common choice. You will learn to place stops at chart levels in chapters 3 and 4.

check.prompt: You buy at $50 with a sell stop at $46. On a normal day with no gap, the price trades down to $45.90. What happens?

options.text: The stop triggers and sells at about $46 or a little lower

check.explanation: Trading at or below $46 triggers a market sell near the stop price.

check.prompt: Your sell stop is at $46. The day closes at $47; the next candle is Open 41, High 42, Low 40.50. Your fill is about:
check.explanation: The price gapped through the stop, so it fills at the open.

check.prompt: The price is $57. You want to buy only if it breaks above $60 resistance. Which real-market order fits?
check.explanation: A buy stop triggers on the break. A buy limit at $60 would fill right away at about $57.

check.prompt: You hold a stop-limit with stop $46 and limit $45.50. The stock gaps down to $41 and the day's high is $42. What happens?

options.text: No fill; you still hold the shares

check.explanation: The stop triggered, but the price never traded at $45.50 or better.

levels.title: The Order Book, Liquidity & Volume
levels.summary: Read the book's depth, see how big orders walk through it, and use volume as a clue.
objectives: Explain liquidity and how big orders walk the book.

terms.definition: How many shares wait at each price in the order book.
The number of shares traded in a period, shown as bars under the chart.
A market with few shares waiting and little trading, so spreads are wide.
When only part of an order executes and the rest waits or is cancelled.

cards.title: The order book
cards.body: The **order book** lists waiting limit orders: bids (buyers) below, asks (sellers) above. The best bid and best ask sit at the top, and the gap between them is the spread. Each line shows a price and how many shares wait there.

cards.title: Depth is liquidity
cards.body: Many shares at each level means a **deep**, liquid market. Few shares means a **thin** one. A big market order eats through level after level, getting a worse price each time. In thin stocks, even a modest order can move the price.

cards.title: Volume
cards.body: **Volume** is the number of shares traded in a period, shown as bars under the chart. High volume means many participants. A 6% jump on three times the usual volume says much more than the same jump on a quiet day.

cards.title: Partial fills
cards.body: In real markets, a large order in a thin stock may fill only in part, with the rest filling later or at worse prices. A good habit is to keep orders small compared with the shares that trade each day. In this game orders fill in full, but some markets have wider spreads.

check.prompt: Bids: $50.00 × 300, $49.95 × 500. Asks: $50.05 × 200, $50.10 × 400. What are the best bid and the spread?
check.explanation: The best bid is the highest bid, $50.00; the best ask is $50.05.

check.prompt: You market-sell 600 shares into that same book. What is your average price?
A stock trading 2,000 shares a day is usually easier to trade in size than one trading 2,000,000 shares a day.
check.explanation: More daily volume usually means more liquidity.

check.prompt: Volume is three times its average while the price jumps 6%. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The price is guaranteed to keep rising
Strong participation, more meaningful than the same move on low volume

check.explanation: High volume shows many traders took part, but it guarantees nothing.
